title: Midshift gut-map: Mirai Ike (runtime candidate) scratch
recommended_next_step: Proceed to a focused take-home: tiny perf debugging + short writeup (2-3 hours). If they decline, do not advance.
content:
Quick context / why I wrote this: met Mirai for 60m loop focused on runtime/operator fit. This is a raw brain dump — impressions, micro-examples, and open questions before we synthesize with panel later.

TL;DR impressions (first-pass):
- Strong systems intuition, especially around tail-latency and backpressure mechanics.
- Lacks depth on modern transformer runtime kernels and low-level CUDA tradeoffs (soft gap).
- Good on observability/telemetry thinking — asked the right questions about sample distributions, SLO budgeting.
- Unclear on ownership/drive for production polish (on-call anecdotes were generic).

Notes by segment (rough):
1) Systems & architecture (30m)
- Walked through a hypothetical hot-path: many small streaming requests -> batching -> KV cache hits + context masking. Mirai sketched a queue/batcher design with per-model size buckets and adaptive timeouts. Good: considered starvation between big/small sequences.
- Mentioned using separate priority lanes and dynamic token budget: pragmatic, team could adopt quickly.
- Asked about degraded-mode: suggested LRU+approximate TTL for KV cache when memory pressure; I pushed on correctness issues w/ stale KV states — she acknowledged complexity but didn't have a concrete reconciliation pattern (gap).
- Called out shard-local telemetry vs global aggregator; recommended exemplar tracing to find cross-shard amplification points. Nice.

2) Performance & low-level (15m)
- When I probed on kernel selection (fused attention, flash-attention), she could explain the high-level tradeoffs (memory vs compute) but stumbled when I asked about specific kernel APIs or how to reason about mixed-precision perf regressions.
- On quantization: understands PTQ vs QAT concepts; limited hands-on experience converting 7B+ models and validating token-level drift. Said they'd pair with ML infra for quant sanity checks.
- Practical perf debugging story: profiled RPC path with flamegraphs, fixed a mutex in scheduler -> 20% tail improvement. Good practical debugging.

3) Observability / SLOs / Incident examples (10m)
- Excellent interviewer-style questions: how to detect model-quality regressions that correlate with infra changes, isolating perf noise vs output drift.
- Shared an incident where a model rollout increased 95th p99 by 60ms — traced to cache eviction behavior. She described experiments she ran to validate hypothesis. Good reproducible thinking.
- On alerting policy: prefers lightweight synthetic probes + canary metrics + request sampling for qualitative checks. Aligned with our approach.

4) Culture / ownership / on-call (5m)
- Mirai's on-call examples were OK but framed as "we had an SRE who handled Kubernetes issues" rather than owning full-stack incident. Not a hard fail but flags whether they'll take product-adjacent ops work.
- Behavioral: calm, collaborative, asks clarifying Qs. Not abrasive.

Green flags (concise):
- Pragmatic batching design and thoughtfulness about fairness across request sizes.
- Good telemetry instincts (exemplar traces, synthetic probes).
- Strong incident postmortem thinking.

Red flags / open gaps:
- Limited low-level kernel/FP32/CUDA fluency — we rely on someone who can read kernels or at least coordinate closely with HPC team.
- Not confident in quantization validation for 7B+ models (we frequently need this knowledge on small teams).
- Limited examples of full-stack ownership during incidents (tendency to rely on ops teams).

Concrete examples she gave (useful soundbites to reference in writeup):
- "We used per-model token windows and adaptive batching — latency-sensitive clients got priority buckets with pre-allocated kernels."
- Took a p99 regression to a mutex; used flamegraphs + contention heatmap to prove it.
- Ran a canary with synthetic prompts + population-matching prompt sets to track quality drift post-quant.

Suggested focused take-home (why + what):
Why: isolates the kernel/telemetry gap without an expensive onsite loop. We need to see: can they find a perf regression in a small reproducible harness, write a short note on root cause, and propose a low-risk mitigation.
What (2–3h):
- Repo with a micro-batcher + toy transformer (we'd provide simple script with an injected perf regression like an accidental global lock or pathological queueing).
- Tasks: run, profile, propose fix, implement minimal change, document method and SLO impact. Also answer 2 short questions: how they'd validate quantization drift and how they'd instrument to detect it in prod.

Scoring breakdown (quick):
- Systems design: 7/10 (good heuristics, bucket-based batching idea is solid)
- Low-level perf/kernel knowledge: 5/10 (can reason, limited hands-on with kernels/quant)
- Observability & incident response: 8/10 (strong)
- Ownership / on-call: 5/10 (needs examples showing proactive full-stack ownership)
- Communication & teamwork: 8/10 (clear, calm, asks good clarifying q's)

Panel talking points (for debrief):
- Recommend take-home focused on perf regression detection/fix. If they demonstrate quick pattern recognition and a reasonable fix, move to final loop.
- If take-home shows persistent inability to reason about kernel-level tradeoffs (e.g., chooses easy but incorrect mitigation like just increasing batch size without addressing lock contention), consider as mismatch for senior runtime engineer role — better fit for infra-focused PM or SWE.

Open questions to ask panel / follow-ups for Mirai if we advance:
- Have them describe a concrete example of touching GPU kernels or working with CUDA teams — pick one and ask for specifics (tools used, numbers, micro-benchmarks).
- Ask for one example where they personally owned an incident end-to-end (pager -> mitigation -> postmortem -> shipped fix). Details matter.

Notes to self / administration:
- Update INF-4821 with our recommended take-home and link test harness.
- Post brief note in #hiring-runtime summarizing TL;DR and suggested ask of candidate (attach harness link).
- If they accept take-home, set 1-week deadline and offer 2h block for questions; code review vs. hand-run evidence OK.

Random scrap (things Mirai said that might be helpful later):
- Likes Prometheus + distributed trace sampling; prefers storing raw tail traces for 24h then downsampling.
- Quick view on caching: "evict cold keys aggressively but keep hot prefixes pinned" — interesting heuristic for prefix caching.

Bottom line: solid candidate with pragmatic instincts and good telemetry/incident thinking. Key risk is low-level kernel/quant depth — take-home will tell us if that's a learning gap or just resume omission. Proceed with targeted take-home.

Action items (my checklist):
- [ ] Draft take-home in INF-4821 (2/13)
- [ ] Ping Mirai with instructions + timeline (D. Ruiz)
- [ ] Share summary in #hiring-runtime and invite panel to review take-home outcome (2/13)

End of note.
